viking1.name: Viking 1 Lander
viking1.realLocation: Chryse Planitia ("Plains of Gold"), northern Mars
viking1.purpose: Take pictures from the surface of Mars and test the soil for signs of life. It was the first US lander to work on Mars.
viking1.howItWorked: A robotic arm scooped up soil and put it into tiny labs inside the lander. The labs heated it, fed it nutrients, and sniffed the gases that came out. Power came from a small nuclear generator, so it did not need sunlight.
viking1.discovery: Three biology experiments found strange chemical activity in the soil, but no clear sign of living things. A separate test found no organic (carbon) molecules. Scientists concluded Viking did not find life, though some details are still discussed today.
viking1.whyStopped: Viking 1 worked for more than 6 years, far longer than the 90 days planned. In November 1982 a faulty command sent from Earth interrupted its communications. Engineers tried for months to wake it up, but it never answered.
viking1.funFact: Just 25 seconds after landing, Viking 1 began sending home the first picture ever taken on the surface of Mars!

sources.label: JPL: Attempts to contact Viking 1 ended

evidenceCard.title: Active Soil
evidenceCard.clue: Mars soil is chemically active, but Viking could NOT prove there is life.

opportunity.name: Opportunity Rover
opportunity.realLocation: Meridiani Planum, near the Martian equator
opportunity.purpose: Be a robot geologist: drive around Mars and read the rocks, looking for clues about whether water was ever there.
opportunity.howItWorked: Solar panels powered six wheels, cameras, and a robotic arm with a rock grinder and a microscope camera. It could grind into a rock and check what it was made of.
opportunity.discovery: Opportunity found tiny round spheres inside layered rock, nicknamed "blueberries" because they look like berries in a muffin (made of the mineral hematite, a mineral that mostly forms when water is around). So, scientists concluded the rock was soaked by liquid water long ago. That is strong evidence that ancient Mars had water.
opportunity.whyStopped: A planet-wide dust storm in June 2018 blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed. Its last signal arrived on 10 June 2018. After more than a thousand recovery commands, NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019.
opportunity.funFact: Opportunity was built to work for about 90 Mars days. It kept going for nearly 15 years, about 60 times longer than planned, and drove more than 45 km (28 miles), farther than a marathon!

sources.label: NASA Astrobiology: Mission comes to an end

evidenceCard.title: Water Rocks
evidenceCard.clue: Some Mars rocks were changed by liquid water a very long time ago.

phoenix.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
phoenix.realLocation: Vastitas Borealis, the icy plains of Mars' far north
phoenix.purpose: Land in the icy far north of Mars, dig into the frozen ground, and find out if there is water ice under the soil.
phoenix.howItWorked: A robotic arm dug shallow trenches in the icy ground. It carried soil to tiny ovens and a mini lab on the lander, which heated it to see what was inside.
phoenix.discovery: Bright, dice-size crumbs showed up in a trench. Four days later they were gone! Salt would have stayed, so it was water ice turning into vapor and floating away. On 31 July 2008 NASA announced that Phoenix had found water in a heated soil sample.
phoenix.whyStopped: Phoenix worked longer than the 90 days planned. But as summer ended, the Sun sank lower and its solar panels made less power. Its last signal came on 2 November 2008, before its power ran out.
phoenix.funFact: Scientists named the trench where the ice vanished "Dodo-Goldilocks".

sources.label: JPL: Bright chunks must have been ice
NASA Photojournal: Phoenix's Lay of the Land

evidenceCard.title: Hidden Ice
evidenceCard.clue: There is frozen water ice on Mars today, just under the soil in the far north.
